title: The Artin-Schreier Theorem: Real-Closed Fields and the FTA
description: The Artin-Schreier theorem (1927) states that F is real-closed if and only if F(sqrt(-1)) is algebraically closed. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (C is algebraically closed) is the special case F = R. This formalization defines real-closed field axioms, verifies R satisfies them, and derives the FTA as a corollary of Artin-Schreier.

meta.author: Artin and Schreier (1927), Gauss (1799)

mathlibDependencies.description: C is algebraically closed (the FTA in Mathlib)

originalContributions: Proof that real-closed fields are not algebraically closed (X^2+1 has no root)
Proof that R satisfies real-closed axioms (using Real.sqrt and sq_nonneg)
FTA derivation chain: R real-closed -> C = R(i) -> Artin-Schreier -> C alg. closed
Universality theorem: FTA is about real-closed fields, not R specifically

overview.historicalContext: Emil Artin and Otto Schreier (1927) introduced the notion of formally real fields and proved that a field is real-closed iff its extension by sqrt(-1) is algebraically closed. This gave a purely algebraic characterization of the property underlying the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, showing that the FTA is not really about R and C specifically, but about the abstract algebraic notion of real-closedness.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question**: Formalize the Artin-Schreier theorem (F real-closed iff F(sqrt(-1)) alg. closed) and show FTA is the special case F = R.

**Result**: We define RealClosedAxioms (pos_sqrt, odd_degree_root, neg_one_not_square), verify R satisfies them, and show the FTA derivation: R real-closed + C = R(i) + Artin-Schreier = C algebraically closed.
overview.text: The Artin-Schreier theorem reveals the FTA as a special case of a general algebraic principle: any real-closed field becomes algebraically closed after a single quadratic extension. R is the standard real-closed field, and C = R(i) is its algebraic closure.
overview.proofStrategy: Define RealClosedAxioms as a structure. Verify R satisfies the axioms using Mathlib (Real.sqrt, sq_nonneg). Define QuadraticExtension for F(sqrt(-1)). Axiomatize Artin-Schreier (both directions). Show C = R(i) is the QuadraticExtension of R. Derive the FTA as a chain: R real-closed -> Artin-Schreier -> C alg. closed.
keyInsights: The FTA is NOT a theorem about R specifically - it's a theorem about real-closed fields
R's only special role is being the 'standard' real-closed field (completion of Q)
Any real-closed field needs exactly one quadratic extension to become algebraically closed
Real-closed = ordered field + IVP for polynomials (odd-degree have roots, positive elements have sqrt)
Contrast with Q: its algebraic closure requires infinitely many extension steps
prerequisites: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (C is algebraically closed)
Ordered fields and the real number system
Square roots and the intermediate value theorem

sections.title: Real-Closed Fields: The Axioms
sections.summary: Defines RealClosedAxioms structure. Proves real-closed fields are not algebraically closed (X^2+1 has no root).
sections.mathContext: A field $F$ is **real-closed** if: (RC1) every positive element has a square root, (RC2) every odd-degree polynomial has a root, (RC3) $-1$ is not a square. Equivalently: $F$ is an ordered field satisfying the intermediate value property for polynomials.

sections.title: The Quadratic Extension F(sqrt(-1))
sections.summary: Defines QuadraticExtension structure. Proves X^2+1 is irreducible over real-closed fields.
sections.mathContext: Given real-closed $F$, form $F(\sqrt{-1}) = F[X]/(X^2+1)$. Since $-1$ is not a square in $F$, $X^2+1$ is irreducible, so $[F(\sqrt{-1}):F] = 2$.

sections.title: The Artin-Schreier Theorem
sections.summary: Axiomatizes both directions of Artin-Schreier. States the equivalence: F real-closed iff F(sqrt(-1)) algebraically closed.
sections.mathContext: **Artin-Schreier (1927)**: $F$ is real-closed $\iff$ $F(\sqrt{-1})$ is algebraically closed. Forward: every polynomial over $F$ factors into linears and quadratics; adjoining $\sqrt{-1}$ splits the quadratics. Backward: algebraic closure of $F(\sqrt{-1})$ provides square roots and odd-degree roots in $F$.

sections.title: R is Real-Closed
sections.summary: Proves R satisfies RC axioms: pos_sqrt via Real.sqrt, neg_one_not_square via sq_nonneg, odd_degree_root axiomated (needs IVT).
sections.mathContext: $\mathbb{R}$ is real-closed: $\sqrt{a}$ exists for $a > 0$ (completeness), odd-degree polynomials have roots (IVT), and $-1 \notin (\mathbb{R})^2$ (since $x^2 \geq 0$). The only axiom needed is the IVT for polynomials.

sections.title: The FTA as a Special Case of Artin-Schreier
sections.summary: Shows C = R(sqrt(-1)) via QuadraticExtension. Derives FTA chain: R real-closed + Artin-Schreier = C alg. closed.
sections.mathContext: The **FTA derivation**: $\mathbb{R}$ is real-closed $\xrightarrow{\text{Artin-Schreier}}$ $\mathbb{R}(\sqrt{-1}) = \mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed. The FTA is not about $\mathbb{R}$ specifically - it holds for any real-closed field.

sections.title: Generalizations: Other Real-Closed Fields
sections.summary: Discusses other real-closed fields: real algebraic numbers, Puiseux series, surreal numbers. States universality: FTA is about real-closed fields in general.
sections.mathContext: Other real-closed fields: $\mathbb{R}_{\text{alg}}$ (real algebraic numbers), $\mathbb{R}((t^{1/\infty}))$ (real Puiseux series), $\textbf{No}$ (Conway's surreal numbers). Each has a corresponding FTA: its quadratic extension is algebraically closed.

conclusion.summary: The Artin-Schreier theorem reveals the FTA as a special case of a general algebraic principle: real-closed fields become algebraically closed after a single quadratic extension by sqrt(-1). R is real-closed (positive sqrt + IVT + -1 not a square), C = R(i) is the quadratic extension, and Artin-Schreier gives algebraic closure.
conclusion.implications: This shifts perspective: the FTA is not a theorem of analysis (despite most proofs using topology or complex analysis). It is fundamentally an algebraic theorem about real-closed fields, with the analytic content isolated in the single fact that R is real-closed.
openQuestions: Can the Artin-Schreier proof (forward direction) be fully formalized in Lean using Galois theory?
What is the constructive content of the Artin-Schreier theorem?
Can real-closed fields be characterized categorically (e.g., as certain model-theoretic structures)?
